method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Ketamine is a safe, effective ED procedural sedation option** — a potent sedative, amnestic, analgesic and anaesthetic.
claims.source_text: Ketamine is a safe and effective procedural sedation option for children in the emergency department setting … Ketamine is a potent sedative, amnestic, analgesic and anaesthetic agent
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Dissociative state:** trance-like with eyes possibly open, muscle tone maintained, effective analgesia, usually total amnesia, **airway reflexes maintained**, BP and heart rate rise slightly; nystagmus and lacrimation are typical.
claims.source_text: Dissociation: the child passes into a trance like state, eyes may be open Catalepsy: normal or slightly increased muscle tone is maintained Analgesia: effective analgesia Amnesia is usually total Airway reflexes are maintained Cardiovascular state: blood pressure and heart rate increase slightly Nystagmus and lacrimation are typical
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use for short, painful procedures, especially needing immobilisation:** lacerations (especially facial), fracture reduction, abscess drainage, foreign-body removal where nitrous oxide is or would be inadequate.
claims.source_text: Ketamine is useful for short, painful procedures, particularly if requiring immobilisation, eg: Lacerations (especially of the face) Fracture reduction Abscess incision & drainage Removal of foreign bodies from eye, ear, nose, skin where nitrous oxide has been or is likely to be inadequate
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Absolute: infants under 3 months.** True allergy is rare; treat as usual allergy/anaphylaxis.
claims.source_text: Absolute Contraindications Infants <3 months Although true allergy is rare, it has been documented and should be treated in accordance with usual allergy/anaphylaxis management
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Relative — discuss with senior staff experienced in sedation:** infants under 12 months (absolute in some jurisdictions, including NSW) · significant current respiratory illness · known difficult airway or previous airway surgery or congenital anomaly · intraoral procedures or bleeding · posterior pharynx stimulation.
claims.source_text: Discuss with senior staff with experience in procedural sedation if any of the following are present: Infants <12 months (absolute contraindication in some jurisdictions, including NSW) Current significant respiratory illness, eg asthma, respiratory tract infection Known difficult airway, history of previous airway surgery or congenital anomaly Intraoral Procedures or potential intraoral bleeding such as tongue lacerations and dental procedures Procedures that will stimulate the posterior pharynx
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Also relative:** cardiovascular disease where a higher heart rate and workload are contraindicated (ischaemic heart disease, cardiac failure, hypertension, Wolff-Parkinson-White) · glaucoma or acute globe injury · porphyria · thyroid disease · bowel obstruction · psychosis.
claims.source_text: Cardiovascular disease where increased HR and workload are contraindicated, eg ischaemic heart disease, cardiac failure, hypertension, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome Glaucoma or acute globe injury Porphyria Thyroid disease Bowel obstruction Psychosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Staff:** senior staff aware and able to help immediately · **one registered nurse** competent in ketamine sedation with annual ALS assessment · **one senior doctor to sedate, credentialed in ketamine sedation and ALS certified** · one doctor to do the procedure. In some settings, including NSW Health, a third credentialled clinician is mandatory.
claims.source_text: Senior staff present in the department must be aware of the sedation, and able to provide immediate assistance if required … One registered nurse capable of airway management and advanced monitoring of child. This nurse must be assessed as competent in ketamine sedation and have completed annual Advanced Life Support (ALS) assessment … One senior doctor to administer the sedation. This doctor must be credentialed in ketamine sedation and ALS certified … One doctor to perform the procedure. … In some health care settings, including NSW health, the presence of a third credentialled clinician is mandatory.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Resuscitation equipment must be readily available. Obtain informed consent**, with baseline BP, HR, RR and oxygen saturation.
claims.source_text: Resuscitation equipment must be readily available … Informed consent must be obtained Baseline observations should include BP, HR, RR and O2 saturation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Non-procedural conversation before and during administration may reduce unpleasant emergence.** Apply topical anaesthetic early — it takes about 45 minutes.
claims.source_text: Facilitate/encourage non-procedural conversation prior and during administration of ketamine … This may help minimise unpleasant emergence phenomena … Apply topical anaesthetic cream early, as it requires approximately 45 minutes to work
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not pre-oxygenate** — it may mask hypoventilation. Fast as per local guidelines.
claims.source_text: Fasting (see local fasting guidelines) Pre-oxygenation is not recommended as may mask hypoventilation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IV is preferred where access is easy:** titratable, shorter recovery, less emesis. **Doses may need adjusting to ideal body weight.**
claims.source_text: Doses may need to be adjusted according to ideal bodyweight … In settings in which IV access can be obtained with minimal upset, the intravenous route is preferable as: The dose can be titrated to effect Shorter recovery time Reduced risk of emesis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IV: 1–1.5 mg/kg over 1–2 minutes immediately before the procedure**, then **0.25–0.5 mg/kg every 10 minutes** as needed. **Maximum 4.5 mg/kg** (rarely needed).
claims.source_text: Initial dose: 1–1.5 mg/kg over 1–2 minutes immediately before the procedure Subsequent incremental dose(s) if needed: 0.25-0.5 mg/kg every 10 minutes until procedure is complete Maximum dose 4.5 mg/kg (though this would be rarely required)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **IV doses over 2.5 mg/kg raise the risk of adverse events** — if more is needed, consider aborting or another sedation option.
claims.source_text: IV doses of >2.5 mg/kg are associated with increased risk of adverse events If doses higher than 2.5 mg/kg are required, consider aborting procedure / explore alternative sedation options
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IM: 4 mg/kg initially (max 6 mg/kg)**; a **repeat 2 mg/kg after 10 minutes** if sedation is inadequate. Ketamine can be used safely without IV access.
claims.source_text: Intramuscular Initial dose of 4 mg/kg (maximum of 6 mg/kg) A repeat dose of 2 mg/kg may be given after 10 minutes if sedation is inadequate Ketamine can be safely used without IV access
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IM vs IV:** onset 3–4 minutes vs 1 minute · effective sedation 15–30 vs 10–20 minutes · average time to discharge 100–140 vs 90–120 minutes.
claims.source_text: Route of Administration IM IV Advantages No IV necessary Ease of repeat dosing, slightly faster recovery Clinical onset 3–4 minutes 1 minute Effective sedation 15–30 minutes 10–20 minutes Time to discharge (average) 100–140 minutes 90–120 minutes
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intranasal ketamine is not currently recommended for procedural sedation** — limited evidence.
claims.source_text: IN ketamine is not currently recommended for procedural sedation due to limited evidence supporting efficacy as a sedation given via IN
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring and a clinician in attendance until recovery is well established**, with close watch on airway and chest movement.
claims.source_text: Each child should have pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring, and a clinician in attendance until recovery is well established Close observation of the airway and chest movements is necessary
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Common and insignificant:** purposeless movements, stiffness, twitching, rash, vocalisation. Tachycardia or hypertension is transient; hypersalivation rarely needs suction.
claims.source_text: Random purposeless movements or stiffness, muscle twitching, rash, and vocalisations: common and of no clinical significance Tachycardia and/or hypertension: transient Hypersalivation: suctioning of hypersalivation may rarely be necessary
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Transient laryngospasm (0.3%)** may need positive-pressure ventilation or RSI; **apnoea or respiratory depression (0.4%)** is usually transient.
claims.source_text: Transient laryngospasm: (0.3%) Positive pressure ventilation may be required, or intubation by Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI) may be considered Apnoea or respiratory depression: (0.4%) is usually transient
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Emesis is more common over 8 years; unpleasant emergence beyond mid-adolescence**, eased by a quiet, low-stimulation room; recovery agitation (1.4%) is uncommon and transient.
claims.source_text: Emesis: more common in children over 8 years therefore suctioning may be necessary Unpleasant emergence phenomena: more common beyond mid adolescence and will resolve in time, a quiet and low stimulation environment may assist Recovery agitation: (1.4%) uncommon and transient
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not discharge until back to premorbid neurological baseline** — able to walk and talk as before. Recover in a quiet, dim area and do not stimulate early.
claims.source_text: The child should not be discharged home until they have returned to their premorbid neurological baseline Nurse in a quiet area with minimal noise and physical contact, allow dim lighting if possible, and do not stimulate prematurely … Child is able to ambulate and verbalise at a level consistent with their premorbid neurological baseline
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If sedation fails**, discuss with senior staff or anaesthetics; the sedation and procedure may need abandoning.
claims.source_text: If ketamine sedation is unsuccessful: Consider discussion with senior staff or anaesthetics, may need to abandon sedation and procedure
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **At home: careful family supervision when mobilising for at least two hours.**
claims.source_text: Careful family observation and supervision if mobilising for at least two hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Ketamine use for procedural sedation' (Last updated December 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Ketamine_use_for_procedural_sedation/, retrieved 2026-09-23
